enonce_markdown: Two walkie-talkies are used by security guards. Only one guard can speak at a time, but each can speak or listen in turn. Which transmission mode is this?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Classify by direction: simplex = one way only; half-duplex = both ways, one at a time; full-duplex = both ways at once.

### Solution

Communication is possible in both directions but not at the same time: **half-duplex**. Simplex would allow one direction only (as in a television broadcast), full-duplex would allow speaking and listening simultaneously (as on a telephone call), and parallel describes how bits are sent along wires, not the direction.

enonce_markdown: Distinguish between serial and parallel transmission, and give **one** reason why serial transmission is preferred over long distances.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Serial sends bits one after another on a single path; parallel sends several bits at the same time on several paths.

### Solution

**Serial:** the bits of a byte are sent one after the other along one wire or channel. **Parallel:** several bits (for example 8) are sent simultaneously, each on its own wire.

Over long distances serial is preferred because: it needs fewer wires, so cables are cheaper; and with parallel lines the signals on different wires arrive at slightly different times (skew) and interfere with each other (crosstalk), which limits the distance and the speed.

enonce_markdown: A file of 15 megabytes (MB) is sent over a link whose data rate is 20 megabits per second (Mbps). Ignoring all overheads, how long does the transfer take? (1 byte = 8 bits.)
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Time = amount of data / data rate, and both must use the same unit: convert bytes to bits.

### Solution

$15\ \text{MB} = 15 \times 8 = 120$ megabits. $t = 120 \div 20 = 6$ s. The value 0.75 s comes from dividing megabytes by megabits per second without converting, 37.5 s from multiplying by 20 and dividing by 8, and 300 s from multiplying 15 by 20.

enonce_markdown: Characters are sent by asynchronous transmission at 9600 bits per second. Each character is framed by 1 start bit, 8 data bits and 1 stop bit (no parity bit). How long does it take to send 1000 characters?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

In asynchronous transmission every character carries its framing bits, so the time is (bits per character x number of characters) / bit rate.

### Solution

Bits per character: $1 + 8 + 1 = 10$. Total bits: $1000 \times 10 = 10\,000$. Time: $10\,000 \div 9600 \approx 1.04$ s. The value 0.83 s counts only the 8 data bits, 1.15 s counts 11 bits per character, and 1.25 s counts 12 bits.

enonce_markdown: Even parity is used on 7-bit characters, the parity bit being added as the eighth (leftmost) bit. (a) Find the parity bit for $1000011$ and for $0110101$. (b) The byte $11001011$ is received. Does it pass the even parity check? (c) Explain why two bits changed in one byte may go unnoticed.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

With even parity, the parity bit is chosen so that the total number of 1s in the byte is even; the receiver counts the 1s.

### Solution

**(a)** $1000011$ has three 1s (odd), so the parity bit is **1**, giving $11000011$. $0110101$ has four 1s (even), so the parity bit is **0**, giving $00110101$.

**(b)** $11001011$ has five 1s (odd), so it **fails** the check: at least one bit has been corrupted.

**(c)** Two flipped bits change the count of 1s by an even number (or none), so the total stays even and the check is passed even though the data are wrong. Parity detects only an odd number of errors and cannot correct them.

enonce_markdown: A file of 1 000 000 bytes is sent over a 56 000 bits per second line. Link A uses asynchronous transmission, with 10 bits sent for every byte. Link B uses synchronous transmission: the file is cut into 1000 blocks of 1000 data bytes, each block carrying 20 extra header bytes, and no start or stop bits. Which link is quicker, and by about how much?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Total time = total bits sent (data plus overhead) / bit rate; compare the overheads of the two methods instead of comparing bit rates only.

### Solution

Link A: $1\,000\,000 \times 10 = 10\,000\,000$ bits, so $t_A = 10\,000\,000 \div 56\,000 \approx 178.6$ s.

Link B: each block has $1020$ bytes, so $1000 \times 1020 \times 8 = 8\,160\,000$ bits and $t_B \approx 145.7$ s.

Link B is faster by $178.6 - 145.7 \approx 33$ s. The value 36 s ignores the headers of link B, and the equal-time option forgets that the number of bits actually sent differs.

choix.texte: Neither: both links take the same time because the bit rate is the same
